Chapman's Homer is George Chapman's English verse translation of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, written in rhymed heroic couplets. Published in folio editions in the early sixteen-tens, Chapman's Iliad became the dominant English Homer for Renaissance and Stuart readers. Though not a literal translation, Chapman's Homer brought the epic vibrantly alive for English speakers and would inspire Keats's famous sonnet on first reading it, standing as the most celebrated English translation until Pope's version in the eighteenth century.

Chapman rendered the text in rhymed heroic couplets, a form that sacrificed classical fidelity for fluidity and natural English speech. He often expanded or condensed Homer freely. He also wrote prefatory essays and glosses, making himself both translator and scholarly guide, attempting to defend Homer's moral philosophy and connect him to Christian virtue. He even filled gaps and completed passages where manuscripts were fragmentary, decisions that influenced how later scholars reconstructed Homer. His style is baroque and ornate, heavy with conceits and Elizabethan-Jacobean diction, quite unlike the simpler directness many modern readers expect from Homer. Keats immortalized the translation in his sonnet "On First Looking into Chapman's Homer," describing the shock of discovery. Chapman's version was eventually superseded by Alexander Pope's Iliad in seventeen fifteen through seventeen twenty, which used couplets with greater elegance and became the standard until the nineteenth century.
